t: Find the Kth Largest Integer in the Array - Ordering Big Numbers as Strings
o: Each number arrives as a string of up to 100 digits, so converting to any fixed-width integer is impossible; comparisons must be done on the strings themselves. For canonical decimal strings without leading zeros, numeric order has a simple form: the longer number is larger, and equal-length numbers compare character by character. In Example 1 the ascending order is ["3","6","7","10"], so the 4th largest - which is just the minimum - is "3". Example 2 shows why naive lexicographic order fails: "12" vs "21" happens to work character-wise, but "2" vs "12" needs the length rule first. Example 3 reminds us duplicates occupy distinct ranks. With up to 10000 strings, either an O(n log n) comparison sort or an O(n log k) bounded heap fits easily.
k: Never parse: comparing the pair (length, lexicographic) reproduces numeric order for canonical decimal strings.
Kth largest with duplicates counted distinctly is an ordinary order statistic on the multiset.
A size-k min-heap always keeps the k largest values seen so far, so its root is the kth largest.

a.n: Approach 1: Sort With a Numeric String Comparator
a.i: Sort all strings with a comparator that first compares lengths and breaks ties lexicographically; this orders them numerically without any conversion. The kth largest is then the element at index n - k in the ascending array. Simple, cache-friendly, and easy to verify.
s: Define compare(a, b): shorter length means smaller; equal lengths use standard string comparison.
Sort the array ascending under this comparator.
Return the element at index len(nums) - k.
a.t: O(n log n * L) - sorting performs O(n log n) comparisons, each costing up to L = 100 characters
a.sp: O(1) extra (or O(n) depending on the language's sort internals)

a.i: Maintain a min-heap under the same numeric ordering, capped at k elements: pushing each new string and evicting the smallest when the size exceeds k leaves exactly the k largest strings, with the global kth largest sitting at the root. This touches far fewer elements than a full sort when k is small relative to n.
s: Create an empty min-heap ordered by (length, lexicographic).
For each string, push it onto the heap.
If the heap size exceeds k, pop the minimum.
After processing everything, return the heap root.
a.t: O(n log k * L) - each of n insertions may sift through log k levels of up-to-L-character comparisons
a.sp: O(k) - the heap never holds more than k strings

w: Present the sort first and offer the heap when k is much smaller than n; if pushed further, quickselect with the same comparator reaches average O(n * L). Pitfalls: comparing strings purely lexicographically ("10" would wrongly precede "9"), converting to Number or long (silent precision loss at 100 digits), and off-by-one between kth largest and index n - k. In JavaScript avoid localeCompare for digit strings since locale collation can surprise; plain < is safe here. Follow-ups: streaming kth largest from a data source (heap), or finding the median of big-number strings.
